title: Iran Is Offering India Oil at $4 a Barrel Below Market Price. India Isn't Sure It Can Say Yes.
excerpt: With sanctions lifted for 60 days and Hormuz traffic picking up, Tehran is flooding Indian refiners with offers — through middlemen, ministers, and the state oil company. The catch: nobody knows how to pay.
body:
The phone calls started within days. After Washington temporarily lifted sanctions on Iranian oil and petrochemicals on June 22, intermediaries from Singapore to Dubai began approaching Indian refiners with an offer that, on paper, looked irresistible: crude oil from Iran, priced $3 to $4 a barrel below comparable regional grades.

The National Iranian Oil Company is making the pitch directly, too. "Apart from NIOC, several traders are contacting us for the sale of Iranian oil. But my priority is to give a chance to NIOC," a senior Indian refining source told Reuters, speaking on condition of anonymity because the discussions are confidential.

And the outreach goes higher. Iranian Petroleum Minister Mohsen Paknejad met India's petroleum minister Hardeep Singh Puri on the sidelines of a recent BRICS energy ministers' meeting to press Tehran's case. Through separate foreign ministry channels, Iran has formally proposed resuming crude sales to New Delhi.

The 60-day sanctions waiver — part of the June 17 interim peace deal between the United States and Iran — has opened a narrow window for energy trade that both countries once took for granted. Before American sanctions were tightened, Iran was among India's top three crude suppliers, and the proximity of Iranian ports to India's western coast kept shipping costs low and delivery times short. That relationship collapsed under sanctions pressure, and China stepped in as Iran's dominant buyer, settling transactions in yuan and gaining outsized leverage over Tehran's pricing.

Now Iran wants out of that dependency. A wider pool of buyers, starting with India, would give Tehran more room to negotiate terms and break China's near-monopoly on its crude exports.

## The Payment Problem


![Hardeep Singh Puri — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4d/Hardeep_Singh_Puri_with_PM_Modi_%28cropped%29.jpg)



> **""The banking framework is the key operational issue now."**



There is a catch, and it is not small. Indian refiners are not sure how to pay for the oil.

The US Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has authorised the sale, but the banking channels and settlement mechanisms remain unclear. No one has spelled out which banks are permitted to handle transactions, what currencies are acceptable, or how Indian institutions can participate without exposing themselves to secondary sanctions risk once the waiver expires.

"The banking framework is the key operational issue now. Once there is clarity on the banks that can participate and the payment arrangements, refiners can take a commercial call," one industry source told The Hindu BusinessLine.

India received two cargoes of Iranian crude in April after a separate 30-day waiver, settling payments in Chinese yuan — a workaround, not a solution. For a sustained trade relationship, both sides need a reliable payment corridor, and neither has one.

## Too Late for This Quarter

Even if the payment mechanics were sorted tomorrow, there is a supply-chain reality that limits how much Iran can sell India in the current window. Indian refiners typically buy crude two months in advance. Most have already secured supplies through August. Middle Eastern term suppliers — Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Kuwait, Iraq — are simultaneously pressing Indian buyers to honour their annual contractual commitments, which were disrupted when the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed after the February 28 strikes.


![New Delhi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg/3840px-Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg)


"Most oil companies are covered till August. We were not expecting a waiver and had already bought whatever was available in the market. In fact, we booked some crude cargoes for August at a premium," a refining source told Reuters.

LPG is a different story. India has already been importing Iranian liquefied petroleum gas through traders, and those flows could increase under the waiver. But here, too, banking clarity will determine the pace.

## The Strategic Calculation

India is approaching the Iranian opening cautiously — and for good reason. The 60-day waiver expires on August 21. If the fragile US-Iran peace talks collapse — and the weekend's tit-for-tat strikes between American and Iranian forces make that a real possibility — any refiner caught mid-transaction could face sanctions exposure. The Doha talks that were supposed to begin this week remain uncertain; Iran's foreign ministry has publicly denied that any direct negotiations with the Americans are scheduled.

Meanwhile, global crude markets are shifting fast. Outbound Persian Gulf exports have rebounded to roughly 75% of pre-war levels. Brent crude, which touched $100 during the war, has fallen to around $73. Cash Dubai has swung from a premium of over $60 a barrel in March to a discount of 27 cents. The oil market, at least for now, is well-supplied.

That softness gives India leverage. With Russian, American, African, and now potentially Iranian crude all competing for Indian demand, New Delhi's refiners can afford to be choosy. They are the world's third-largest oil importer, and every major producer wants their business.

## What the Diaspora Should Watch

For the nine million Indians working in the Gulf — and for every NRI household sending remittances home from a petrodollar economy — the oil price trajectory matters directly. Cheaper oil strengthens the Indian rupee, lowers the current account deficit, and reduces inflationary pressure on everything from cooking gas to freight costs. But a collapsed peace deal could reverse all of that within days.

The broader question is whether India can navigate the narrow channel between cheap Iranian crude and geopolitical risk. It has done this before — and been burned. This time, the refiners seem determined to let the diplomats go first.
